entries.meaning: A building where Christians meet to worship. ---
examples: There's a little white church at the end of the road.
We go to church every Sunday morning.
Half the churches in town run a food pantry.

entries.meaning: A building where Jews gather for prayer and study. ---
examples: Her family belongs to a synagogue downtown.
The synagogue holds classes on Wednesday evenings.
Both synagogues took part in the memorial service.

entries.meaning: A small place of worship, often inside a larger building. ---
examples: The hospital has a quiet chapel on the first floor.
They were married in a tiny chapel in the mountains.
Most of the college chapels are open to the public.

entries.meaning: A building where monks live and work together. ---
examples: The monastery sits high above the valley.
He spent two years at a monastery in Kentucky.
Several monasteries in the area make and sell cheese.

entries.meaning: A building where nuns live together. ---
examples: Her aunt entered a convent at nineteen.
The old convent is now a school.
Two convents closed when the sisters grew too few.

entries.meaning: The holy main room of a place of worship, or any place of safety. ---
examples: The choir sang from the back of the sanctuary.
The old church became a sanctuary for people with nowhere to go.
These islands are sanctuaries for nesting birds.

entries.meaning: The raised platform a preacher speaks from in a church. ---
examples: He stepped up to the pulpit and opened his notes.
The pulpit is carved out of dark oak.
Politics is preached from a lot of pulpits these days.
entries.contrast: The first syllable has the vowel of 'pull', not of 'pulp': PUUL-pit.

entries.meaning: A raised table used for religious ceremonies. ---
examples: Two candles burned on the altar.
She walked up to the altar in her mother's dress.
The museum displays stone altars from ancient temples.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like the verb 'alter' (изменять). The noun ends in -ar.

entries.meaning: A long wooden bench for people to sit on in a church. ---
examples: We squeezed into the last pew in the back.
There's a hymnbook in the rack on every pew.
The pews were packed for the Christmas service.

entries.meaning: A piece of ground where dead people are buried. ---
examples: His grandparents are buried in the town cemetery.
We drove past a small country cemetery.
Two of the city's cemeteries date from the 1800s.
entries.contrast: Spelled with three e's and no a: c-e-m-e-t-e-r-y.

entries.meaning: A stone structure built to hold a dead body. ---
examples: The tomb was sealed for two thousand years.
Visitors leave coins on the tomb.
Archaeologists opened three tombs that winter.
entries.contrast: The b is silent; the word rhymes with 'room', not with 'bomb'.

entries.meaning: A man trained to lead religious services in a church or temple. ---
examples: A young priest heard her confession.
The priest blessed the bread and the wine.
Two priests were sent to the new parish.

entries.meaning: A Christian leader in charge of a local church. ---
examples: Our pastor has been here for twelve years.
The pastor visited him in the hospital.
Several pastors spoke at the rally.

entries.meaning: A Jewish religious leader and teacher. ---
examples: The rabbi welcomed everyone in Hebrew and English.
She studied with a rabbi for a year before converting.
Local rabbis signed the letter together.
entries.contrast: The last syllable rhymes with 'eye': RAB-eye, not 'RAB-ee'.

entries.meaning: A Muslim leader who directs prayers in a mosque. ---
examples: The imam gave a short talk after prayers.
He asked the imam what the verse meant.
Two imams joined the interfaith meeting.

entries.meaning: A man who lives in a religious community under strict rules. ---
examples: A monk met us at the gate.
He lived as a monk for eight years.
The monks get up at four in the morning.

entries.meaning: A senior Christian clergyman in charge of many churches. ---
examples: The bishop came to confirm the teenagers.
A letter from the bishop was read aloud.
The bishops meet twice a year.

entries.meaning: The head of the Roman Catholic Church. ---
examples: The pope spoke to the crowd from the balcony.
She waited six hours to see the pope.
Several popes are buried beneath the church.

entries.meaning: Someone who gives religious talks to a group of people. ---
examples: The preacher spoke for almost an hour.
His father was a country preacher.
Street preachers stand on that corner every Saturday.

entries.meaning: A clergy member who serves an army unit, hospital, prison, or school. ---
examples: The hospital chaplain sat with the family all night.
He served as an army chaplain in the 1990s.
The prison employs two full-time chaplains.
entries.contrast: The second syllable is a weak -lin, not 'plane': CHAP-lin.

entries.meaning: Someone sent to another place to spread a religion and help people. ---
examples: Her parents worked as a missionary couple in Brazil.
A missionary built the first school in the village.
Young missionaries knocked on our door Saturday morning.

entries.meaning: A preacher who travels around trying to convert people to Christianity. ---
examples: A traveling evangelist filled the stadium.
The evangelist broadcasts his sermons on the radio.
TV evangelists raised millions that year.

entries.meaning: A person believed to speak messages from God. ---
examples: The prophet warned the city to change its ways.
He read the words of an ancient prophet.
The prophets are quoted throughout the book.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'profit' (прибыль); only the spelling differs.

entries.meaning: A person officially recognized as holy after death. ---
examples: She was made a saint four centuries later.
There's a statue of the saint by the door.
The church is named after two saints.

entries.meaning: A follower who learns from and believes in a teacher or leader. ---
examples: He was a disciple of the old master painter.
The story tells how one disciple doubted.
Twelve disciples sat down at the table.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, unlike 'discipline' (DISS-uh-plin).

entries.meaning: One of the first followers sent out to teach a religion. ---
examples: The letter was written by an apostle.
That window shows the apostle with a set of keys.
The apostles traveled from town to town.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: uh-PAH-suhl.

entries.meaning: Someone who accepts a religion or idea as true. ---
examples: She's a firm believer in second chances.
The speaker was preaching to believers only.
Millions of believers fast during that month.

entries.meaning: The group of people who attend a particular place of worship. ---
examples: The whole congregation stood to sing.
Our congregation has grown by fifty families.
Small rural congregations are shrinking every year.

entries.meaning: Someone who travels to a holy place for religious reasons. ---
examples: A tired pilgrim asked for water at the door.
Every pilgrim carries a small shell as a sign.
Thousands of pilgrims walk the road each spring.

entries.meaning: Someone killed because of their religious or political beliefs. ---
examples: He died a martyr at the age of thirty.
The church honors her as a martyr.
Statues of the martyrs stand along the wall.
entries.contrast: The -yr sounds like -ter: MAR-tur, not 'mar-TEER'.

entries.meaning: Someone who believes that no god exists. ---
examples: He's been an atheist since college.
The atheist and the priest ended up friends.
Atheists make up a small share of the population.
entries.contrast: First syllable is AY-, not 'AH-': AY-thee-ist.

entries.meaning: Someone who thinks it is impossible to know whether a god exists. ---
examples: She calls herself an agnostic rather than an atheist.
As an agnostic, he avoids the question entirely.
Both agnostics and believers filled out the survey.

entries.meaning: The people ordained to lead religious services, taken as a group. ---
examples: Members of the clergy were invited to speak.
The clergy have asked the city for help.
He left the clergy after twenty years.
entries.contrast: No plural form, and it takes a plural verb: 'the clergy were', not 'was'.

entries.meaning: A person who breaks religious or moral law. ---
examples: He called himself a sinner in need of mercy.
The sermon was aimed at every sinner in the room.
Sinners and saints sat in the same pews.

entries.meaning: Someone who has changed to a new religion or belief. ---
examples: He's a recent convert to Islam.
The church welcomed the new convert by name.
Most of the converts were young adults.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable (KAHN-vurt); the verb stresses the second (kuhn-VURT).

entries.meaning: A woman believed to have magic powers. ---
examples: In the story a witch curses the whole village.
She dressed as a witch for Halloween.
Twenty people were hanged as witches.
entries.contrast: For most Americans this sounds exactly like 'which'.

entries.meaning: A person who follows the religion based on Jesus Christ. ---
examples: He was raised a Christian but stopped going to church.
As a Christian, she takes the commandment seriously.
Christians make up most of the town.

entries.meaning: A member of the Christian church led by the pope. ---
examples: Her husband is a Catholic from Boston.
He was the first Catholic elected president.
Catholics and Protestants share the holiday.

entries.meaning: A member of a Christian church that separated from Rome. ---
examples: Most of her neighbors are Protestants.
His grandfather was a Protestant from a small Ohio town.
American Protestants belong to dozens of denominations.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, unlike the verb 'protest' (pruh-TEST).

entries.meaning: A person who follows the religion of Islam. ---
examples: A Muslim at my office explained the fast to me.
She's the first Muslim on the city council.
Muslims pray five times a day.

entries.meaning: A member of the Jewish people or a follower of Judaism. ---
examples: His grandfather was a Jew from Odessa.
As a Jew, he grew up going to synagogue.
Jews around the world celebrate the holiday.

entries.meaning: A person who follows the teachings of the Buddha. ---
examples: She became a Buddhist in her forties.
A Buddhist from the temple led the meditation.
Buddhists in the area share one small temple.
entries.contrast: The dd is one sound and the h is silent: BOO-dist.

entries.meaning: A person who follows the religion of Hinduism. ---
examples: Our doctor is a Hindu from Chennai.
A Hindu runs the shop next door.
Many Hindus do not eat beef.

entries.meaning: Belief in and worship of a god, or an organized system of such belief. ---
examples: They never argue about politics or religion.
Islam is the second largest religion in the world.
The class compares five world religions.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The religion based on the life and teachings of Jesus Christ. ---
examples: Christianity spread quickly through the empire.
He converted to Christianity as an adult.
The course covers the early history of Christianity.

entries.meaning: The religion of Muslims, based on the teachings of Muhammad. ---
examples: Islam is practiced by well over a billion people.
She wrote her thesis on art in early Islam.
He learned about Islam from a friend at work.

entries.meaning: The religion of the Jewish people. ---
examples: Judaism is one of the oldest living religions.
She converted to Judaism before the wedding.
The exhibit traces Judaism in America.

entries.meaning: The religion based on the teachings of the Buddha. ---
examples: Buddhism reached China along the trade routes.
He got interested in Buddhism through meditation.
Buddhism has many different schools.

entries.meaning: The main religion of India, with many gods and sacred texts. ---
examples: Hinduism has no single founder.
The festival comes out of Hinduism.
She teaches a class on Hinduism and its texts.

entries.meaning: A branch of a religion with its own organization and beliefs. ---
examples: Their denomination ordains women.
He switched to a smaller denomination.
Twelve Christian denominations signed the letter.

entries.meaning: A small religious group that has broken away from a larger one. ---
examples: The sect keeps to itself in the hills.
A strict sect founded the settlement in 1830.
Rival sects have argued over the text for centuries.

entries.meaning: A religious group with unusual beliefs and a powerful leader. ---
examples: Her brother joined a cult in his twenties.
The cult cut its members off from their families.
Reporters spent years investigating both cults.

entries.meaning: The study of God and religious belief. ---
examples: He studied theology before going to law school.
Her theology is more forgiving than his.
The argument is about theology, not politics.

entries.meaning: A belief or set of beliefs taught by a church or other authority. ---
examples: The doctrine has not changed in centuries.
He questioned one doctrine and was asked to leave.
The two churches differ on several doctrines.

entries.meaning: Belief that a group insists is true and refuses to question. ---
examples: He has no patience for religious dogma.
The article attacks economic dogma as much as church dogma.
What began as an idea hardened into dogma.

entries.meaning: A short statement of the beliefs of a religion. ---
examples: The congregation recited the creed together.
Honesty was the old man's whole creed.
The two churches use slightly different creeds.

entries.meaning: Strong belief without proof, or a particular religion. ---
examples: She kept her faith through all of it.
He was raised in the Jewish faith.
Leaders of several faiths attended the service.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The holy book of Christianity. ---
examples: There's a Bible in the drawer of every nightstand.
He read the whole Bible in a year.
The hotel gave away hundreds of Bibles.

entries.meaning: The sacred writings of a religion. ---
examples: He backed up every point with scripture.
The passage is one of the best known in scripture.
They study scripture on Tuesday nights.

entries.meaning: One of the four books telling the life of Jesus, or the message itself. ---
examples: She read a few verses from the gospel.
He preached the gospel for forty years.
The four gospels tell the story differently.

entries.meaning: Either of the two main parts of the Christian Bible. ---
examples: That story comes from the Old Testament.
He knows the New Testament almost by heart.
The class reads both testaments in translation.

entries.meaning: A rule given by God that people must obey. ---
examples: Which commandment comes first?
He broke the commandment about bearing false witness.
The Ten Commandments were carved on the wall.

entries.meaning: A short story told to teach a moral or religious lesson. ---
examples: He answered with a parable about a lost sheep.
The parable of the good Samaritan is famous.
Jesus taught in parables.

entries.meaning: A sacred song or poem, especially one from the Book of Psalms. ---
examples: She read a psalm at the funeral.
The choir sang a psalm in Latin.
There are a hundred and fifty psalms.
entries.contrast: Both the p and the l are silent: SAHM.

entries.meaning: The holy book of Islam. ---
examples: He keeps a Quran on the top shelf.
She has memorized long passages of the Quran.
The mosque hands out free Qurans in English.
entries.contrast: Also spelled 'Koran' in older American books; the pronunciation is the same.

entries.meaning: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible, holy to Jews. ---
examples: The Torah is read aloud on Saturday mornings.
He studies Torah every week with a partner.
The scroll of the Torah is written by hand.

entries.meaning: A talk on a religious or moral subject given in a service. ---
examples: The sermon ran long and the kids got restless.
Her sermon was about forgiving your neighbors.
He posts his sermons online every week.

entries.meaning: Words spoken to God, or the act of speaking to God. ---
examples: She said a short prayer before the meal.
The family turned to prayer that night.
Our prayers are with you.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: One syllable in American English, rhyming with 'there' — not two syllables like 'player'.

entries.meaning: The showing of love and respect for a god through prayer and ceremony. ---
examples: The building has been used for worship since 1840.
Sunday worship starts at ten.
The law protects freedom of worship.

entries.meaning: God's favor, or words asking for it. ---
examples: The priest gave the couple his blessing.
Losing that job turned out to be a blessing.
She counts her blessings every night.

entries.meaning: A Christian ceremony in which water is used to accept someone into the church. ---
examples: The whole family came for the baptism.
His baptism took place in a river.
The church records list every baptism since 1902.

entries.meaning: The Christian ceremony of sharing bread and wine. ---
examples: They take communion on the first Sunday of the month.
She received her first communion at eight.
Communion is offered at the end of the service.

entries.meaning: A set of actions always performed the same way, often for religious reasons. ---
examples: The ritual has been passed down for generations.
Coffee on the porch is his morning ritual.
The book describes wedding rituals around the world.

entries.meaning: A formal religious ceremony with fixed words and actions. ---
examples: The priest performed the last rite at the bedside.
Getting a driver's license is an American rite of passage.
Burial rites differ from culture to culture.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'right' and 'write'.

entries.meaning: A formal event held to mark an important occasion. ---
examples: The wedding ceremony lasted twenty minutes.
She spoke at the graduation ceremony.
Both ceremonies were held outdoors.
entries.contrast: Americans give the third syllable a full 'moh': SEH-ruh-moh-nee; the British say SERR-uh-muh-nee.

entries.meaning: Money or a gift presented as part of worship. ---
examples: They collect the offering halfway through the service.
He dropped a folded bill into the offering.
Small offerings of fruit were left at the shrine.

entries.meaning: A tenth of a person's income given to a church. ---
examples: He pays a tithe every month.
The tithe keeps the building running.
Tithes used to be collected in grain.
entries.contrast: The th is voiced, as in 'bathe', not as in 'thin'.

entries.meaning: Money or food given to poor people as a religious duty. ---
examples: Giving alms is one of the pillars of Islam.
Beggars sat by the gate asking for alms.
The monks lived entirely on alms.
entries.contrast: The l is silent, and there is no singular form 'alm'.

entries.meaning: The practice of sitting quietly and focusing the mind. ---
examples: He does twenty minutes of meditation every morning.
Meditation helped her sleep better.
The retreat teaches meditation to beginners.

entries.meaning: Going without food, often for religious reasons. ---
examples: Fasting during daylight hours is required that month.
The doctor asked whether the fasting was safe for him.
She gave up fasting after her surgery.

entries.meaning: The ceremony held when someone is buried or cremated. ---
examples: The funeral is at eleven on Thursday.
Almost the whole town came to the funeral.
He's been to three funerals this year.
entries.contrast: English uses a singular 'a funeral' where Russian uses the plural 'похороны'.

entries.meaning: A period of staying awake to pray or to remember someone. ---
examples: Hundreds gathered for a candlelight vigil.
She kept a vigil by his hospital bed.
Vigils were held in a dozen cities.

entries.meaning: An upright shape with a bar across it, the main symbol of Christianity. ---
examples: She wears a small gold cross.
A wooden cross stands on the hill.
White crosses mark the graves.

entries.meaning: A cross with a figure of Jesus on it. ---
examples: A crucifix hung above the door.
He held the crucifix in both hands.
The shop sells rosaries and crucifixes.

entries.meaning: A substance burned to make a sweet smell during worship. ---
examples: The whole church smelled of incense.
She lit a stick of incense on the shelf.
They burn incense before the morning chant.
entries.contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable (IN-senss); the verb 'to incense' (привести в ярость) stresses the second (in-SENSS).

entries.meaning: A painted religious image, especially in Orthodox churches. ---
examples: An old icon hung in the corner of the room.
The icon is painted on wood with gold leaf.
The museum holds two hundred Russian icons.

entries.meaning: A statue worshipped as a god, or a person admired too much. ---
examples: The prophet told them to break the idol.
That guitarist was his idol growing up.
Stone idols were found under the temple floor.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'idle' (праздный, незанятый).

entries.meaning: An object kept because it belonged to a holy person or an earlier time. ---
examples: The church claims to hold a relic of the saint.
That typewriter is a relic from another century.
The relics are kept in a locked case.

entries.meaning: A string of beads used to count prayers, or the set of prayers itself. ---
examples: She keeps a rosary in her purse.
They said the rosary together every evening.
He carved wooden rosaries to sell at the market.

entries.meaning: A large boat or sacred chest described in the Bible. ---
examples: The children drew animals lining up for the ark.
The scrolls are kept in the ark at the front of the synagogue.
Model arks are a favorite in Sunday school.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'arc' (дуга).

entries.meaning: A small round cap worn by Jewish men. ---
examples: He put on a yarmulke before entering.
Her son's yarmulke is held on with a clip.
A basket of yarmulkes sits by the door.
entries.contrast: The r in the spelling is not pronounced: YAH-muh-kuh.

entries.meaning: A being believed to have power over nature and human life. ---
examples: He prayed to a god he wasn't sure existed.
Thunder was said to be the voice of a god.
The Greeks had dozens of gods.

entries.meaning: A female god. ---
examples: The temple was built for a goddess of the harvest.
She was named after a goddess.
Statues of three goddesses line the hall.

entries.meaning: A god or goddess. ---
examples: Each village honored a local deity.
The carving shows a deity with four arms.
Hundreds of deities appear in the old stories.
entries.contrast: The first syllable is DEE-, not 'DAY-'.

entries.meaning: Someone who rescues people from danger or from sin. ---
examples: Christians call Jesus their savior.
The new coach was treated like a savior.
The town has had a few would-be saviors over the years.
entries.contrast: American spelling is 'savior'; the British write 'saviour'.

entries.meaning: A leader expected to come and save a people. ---
examples: They believed the messiah would come in their lifetime.
Voters were looking for a messiah, not a manager.
History is full of false messiahs.

entries.meaning: The spiritual part of a person, believed to live on after death. ---
examples: She prayed for his soul.
There wasn't a soul on the street.
The old hymn is about lost souls finding their way home.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like 'sole' (подошва; единственный).

entries.meaning: A being without a body, or the non-physical part of a person. ---
examples: They believe a spirit watches over the house.
His body was weak but his spirit wasn't.
The story is full of forest spirits.

entries.meaning: A spiritual being that serves as a messenger of God. ---
examples: An angel appears to the shepherds in the story.
The nurse was an absolute angel.
Carved angels look down from the ceiling.
entries.contrast: AYN-juhl, not to be confused with 'angle' (ANG-guhl, угол).

entries.meaning: An evil spirit, or the chief evil spirit in Christianity. ---
examples: He says the devil is in the details.
The painting shows a devil with a pitchfork.
Little devils, she called the twins.

entries.meaning: An evil spirit believed to harm or possess people. ---
examples: The priest claimed to have driven out a demon.
In the film a demon haunts the family.
He's still fighting his own demons.

entries.meaning: The spirit of a dead person, believed to appear to the living. ---
examples: She swears she saw a ghost on the stairs.
The hotel is supposed to have a ghost.
He doesn't believe in ghosts.
entries.contrast: The h after the g is silent: GOHST.

entries.meaning: The place where God lives and good people are believed to go after death. ---
examples: She believes her mother is in heaven.
That first cup of coffee was heaven.
Thank heaven you called.

entries.meaning: The place of punishment after death in some religions. ---
examples: The sermon was mostly about hell.
That drive in August was pure hell.
He went through hell to get here.

entries.meaning: A perfect place of happiness, especially the home of the blessed after death. ---
examples: The garden is described as paradise.
They believe the faithful enter paradise.
Two weeks on that island was paradise.

entries.meaning: Life believed to continue after death. ---
examples: He doesn't believe in the afterlife.
The book is about what different religions say about the afterlife.
Her faith in the afterlife comforted the family.

entries.meaning: The act of coming back to life after death. ---
examples: Easter celebrates the resurrection.
The whole faith rests on the resurrection.
The sermon focused on the resurrection and what it means.

entries.meaning: Being saved from sin and its punishment. ---
examples: The preacher spoke about salvation through faith.
She found salvation in the church basement, she says.
That loan was his salvation.

entries.meaning: An act that breaks a religious or moral law. ---
examples: Lying to her was his worst sin.
It's a sin to waste food like that.
He confessed his sins and asked for forgiveness.

entries.meaning: God's free kindness toward people who do not earn it. ---
examples: The hymn is about grace and forgiveness.
He believes he was saved by grace alone.
They prayed for the grace to forgive him.

entries.meaning: Kindness shown to someone you have the power to punish. ---
examples: The prisoner begged for mercy.
She showed him no mercy in the debate.
God's mercy is the theme of the whole psalm.

entries.meaning: The act of stopping being angry at someone for a wrong. ---
examples: He asked his brother for forgiveness.
Forgiveness took her years.
The whole sermon was about forgiveness.

entries.meaning: An event that cannot be explained by natural law, seen as the work of God. ---
examples: The doctors called her recovery a miracle.
It's a miracle nobody was hurt.
The gospel describes several miracles.

entries.meaning: A statement about what will happen, said to come from God. ---
examples: The old prophecy mentioned a great flood.
His prophecy turned out to be right.
The book is full of prophecies about the end of the world.
entries.contrast: The noun 'prophecy' ends in -see; the verb 'prophesy' ends in -sigh.

entries.meaning: A truth made known, especially one believed to come from God. ---
examples: He described the moment as a revelation.
The prophet claimed a revelation from God.
The report contained some ugly revelations.

entries.meaning: Words meant to bring evil on someone, or the evil that follows. ---
examples: The family believed there was a curse on the house.
Fame turned out to be a curse.
The novel is full of ancient curses.

entries.meaning: A belief that certain actions bring good or bad luck. ---
examples: Not walking under ladders is an old superstition.
He calls it tradition; she calls it superstition.
Baseball players have all kinds of superstitions.

entries.meaning: An old story about gods and heroes, or a widely believed false idea. ---
examples: The myth explains where fire came from.
That's a myth — sugar doesn't make kids hyper.
The class reads Greek myths all semester.

entries.meaning: The power believed to decide events, or what happens to a particular person. ---
examples: She believes everything happens by fate.
He met the same fate as his father.
The fates of the two families were tied together.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The belief that a person's actions decide what happens to them later. ---
examples: He says his good karma finally caught up with him.
Karma is central to both Hinduism and Buddhism.
Cutting people off in traffic is bad karma.

entries.meaning: The belief that a soul is born again in a new body after death. ---
examples: Reincarnation is a central idea in Hinduism.
She half believes in reincarnation.
The film plays with the idea of reincarnation.

entries.meaning: A state of complete spiritual understanding. ---
examples: The Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment under a tree.
He spent years searching for enlightenment.
Enlightenment, the teacher said, is not a prize.

entries.meaning: In Buddhism, the perfect peace reached when suffering and desire end. ---
examples: The goal is to reach nirvana.
For him a quiet Sunday is nirvana.
The book explains what nirvana actually means.

entries.meaning: Deep love and loyalty, especially toward a god or a person. ---
examples: Her devotion to her students was obvious.
The shrine is a place of quiet devotion.
He cared for his wife with total devotion.

entries.meaning: Speech that shows disrespect for God or sacred things. ---
examples: He was accused of blasphemy.
Around here, criticizing the team is blasphemy.
The law against blasphemy was repealed long ago.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable: BLASS-fuh-mee, not 'blas-FEE-mee'.

entries.meaning: In Catholic belief, a place where souls are cleansed before heaven. ---
examples: Catholic teaching describes purgatory as temporary.
The airport at midnight felt like purgatory.
Souls in purgatory are prayed for by the living.

entries.meaning: The complete destruction of the world, especially as described in the Bible. ---
examples: The book describes the apocalypse in strange images.
Half of Hollywood has filmed some kind of apocalypse.
The two novels imagine very different apocalypses.

entries.meaning: A strong wish to do something you know is wrong. ---
examples: He gave in to temptation and bought it anyway.
The story is about resisting temptation.
The city is full of temptations.

entries.meaning: The inner sense that tells a person right from wrong. ---
examples: His conscience wouldn't let him keep the money.
She has a clear conscience about it.
The decision weighed on both their consciences.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with 'conscious' (KAHN-shuhs, в сознании) — different word, different ending.

entries.meaning: A sign believed to show what will happen in the future. ---
examples: A black cat was once considered a bad omen.
Rain on your wedding day is a good omen in some places.
The sailors read the clouds for omens.

entries.meaning: Something a culture forbids people to do or even mention. ---
examples: Talking about money is still a taboo in her family.
Eating pork is a taboo in several religions.
The film breaks a few old taboos.

entries.meaning: The use of supposed supernatural power to make things happen. ---
examples: The villagers believed she worked magic.
He does card magic at birthday parties.
It looked like magic from where I was standing.
entries.contrast: Uncountable: you say 'she does magic', never 'magics'.

entries.meaning: The practice of magic, especially harmful magic. ---
examples: She was accused of witchcraft in 1692.
The trials for witchcraft lasted a year.
Belief in witchcraft was widespread at the time.

entries.meaning: The belief that the stars and planets influence people's lives. ---
examples: She reads about astrology but doesn't take it seriously.
Astrology columns still run in some newspapers.
He can't tell astrology from astronomy.
entries.contrast: Astrology is about horoscopes; astronomy (uh-STRAH-nuh-mee) is the science of the stars.

entries.meaning: The weekly day of rest and worship in Judaism and Christianity. ---
examples: They don't drive on the Sabbath.
The store used to close for the Sabbath.
Keeping the Sabbath is one of the commandments.

entries.meaning: The Christian holiday celebrating the return of Jesus to life. ---
examples: We always dye eggs before Easter.
Easter falls in late March this year.
The kids hunt for candy on Easter morning.

entries.meaning: The Christian holiday celebrating the birth of Jesus. ---
examples: We drive to my parents' house every Christmas.
The store puts up decorations before Christmas.
Christmas is on a Wednesday this year.
entries.contrast: The t is silent: KRISS-muhss.

entries.meaning: The Muslim holy month of fasting from dawn to sunset. ---
examples: Ramadan begins next week.
He fasts every day during Ramadan.
The mosque serves a free meal each night of Ramadan.

entries.meaning: The Jewish holiday remembering the escape from slavery in Egypt. ---
examples: The whole family gathers for Passover.
She cleans the kitchen before Passover.
Passover lasts eight days.

entries.meaning: The Jewish festival of lights, lasting eight nights.
examples: They light one more candle each night of Hanukkah.
Hanukkah starts in December this year.
We ate potato pancakes for Hanukkah.
